content: Free-range eggs are distinct from factory-farmed eggs primarily because the hens are allowed to roam freely within the farmyard during the day and are only confined to sheds or henhouses at night. However, not all countries have legal definitions or standards for what constitutes free-range. For instance, in the United States, the Department of Agriculture does not enforce specific standards, allowing egg producers to label any eggs as free-range without strict oversight. Some producers may also use the term cage-free either alongside or instead of free-range. In contrast, countries like Australia have stringent regulations that define what qualifies as free-range. Eggs that do not meet these criteria must explicitly state on their packaging that they are cage-laid or barn-laid. Consumers who prefer free-range eggs often seek products from hens raised under traditional, low-density free-range farming methods. Critics of European Union-style free-range regulations argue that commercial free-range egg farming often fails to meet these consumer expectations. This is because such regulations permit yarding, a practice that combines high-density poultry housing with a fenced outdoor yard. Yarding is closer in practice and outcome to high-density confinement systems than to true free-range farming. Free-range eggs may have broader yolks with a more orange hue, which is attributed to the hens' diet rich in greens and insects. However, an orange yolk does not necessarily indicate that the egg was produced by a free-range hen. Feed additives, such as marigold petal meal, dried algae, or alfalfa meal, can artificially enhance yolk color. Nutritionally, eggs from genuine free-range hens—those that forage daily on grass pastures—are superior to eggs from other hens. They contain significantly higher levels of Omega-3 fatty acids and vitamins A and E, while also having lower levels of total fat, saturated fat, cholesterol, and Omega-6 fatty acids.
